vignette:
He is a 72-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes to therapy with a careful, measured way of speaking, as if he has learned over many years that taking up too much space can be dangerous. He is married now, and his life looks stable from the outside. He works as a nanny, a role he describes with quiet pride, caring for young children in a home that feels orderly and safe. He is gentle with them, patient in the way he wishes someone had once been patient with him. He says that being around children is soothing because they need simple things-food, attention, reassurance-and do not ask him to explain what he would rather keep hidden.

When he was younger, he lives for a time with a romantic partner who becomes physically abusive. He does not describe the beginning of the relationship as terrible. At first, he remembers feeling grateful to be wanted, relieved to have companionship, and hopeful that love might make his life feel less lonely. The violence arrives gradually, then all at once. A shove becomes a slap, a slap becomes being pinned against a wall, and then there are blows that leave marks he learns to conceal. He becomes skilled at reading a room in an instant: the set of a jaw, the sound of footsteps, the change in breathing that tells him danger is close. He learns to apologize quickly, to stay small, to anticipate what might set the other person off. Over time, he stops trusting his own judgment because nothing he does seems to prevent the next assault.

Even now, decades later, he speaks of those years in fragments. He remembers the texture of fear more clearly than the details of the blows. At night, he would lie awake listening for movement in the house, his body rigid, waiting. During the day he would work, smile, nod, and keep going as if nothing were wrong. He says he became expert at looking normal. This habit has stayed with him. In session he often minimizes what happened, then pauses, looking down at his hands as if he has just realized how much effort it takes to keep the story contained.

After he leaves the abusive relationship, he expects that the worst is behind him. Instead, the fear follows him in quieter forms. He startles easily at sudden sounds. Raised voices, even in a movie or from neighbors, send a rush of heat through his chest. His muscles tighten before he can think. When someone steps too close behind him, he feels an immediate need to turn, to create distance. He avoids arguments whenever possible, even with people who care about him, because conflict makes his mind go blank and his body feel as though it is bracing for impact. At times, he has sudden images of being trapped again, and he struggles to sleep because his thoughts become busy after dark. He wakes feeling already tired, as if he has spent the night on watch.

He does not talk much about anger, but it is present in the way he describes himself. He is angry that he had to survive by shrinking. He is angry that his body still reacts as if the danger is current. He is also ashamed of how long he stayed. That shame surfaces most when he thinks about intimacy and trust. Even in his marriage, which he experiences as caring and steady, there are moments when closeness makes him tense. He wants affection, yet part of him expects it to turn painful. He often tests the safety of a situation before relaxing into it, watching for signs that a person's mood may change. His wife has come to understand that his silence is not withdrawal from her, but a kind of vigilance he has never fully been able to put down.

As a nanny, he is especially attentive to children's emotions. He notices quickly when a child is frightened or overstimulated. He kneels to their level, softens his voice, and tries to make the world feel less threatening. There is something reparative for him in offering the steadiness he once needed. Still, certain moments at work unsettle him-a child reaching suddenly, a toy crashing to the floor, a parent speaking sharply in another room. In those moments, he feels his heart pound and his attention narrow until he can reorient himself. He recovers by focusing on practical tasks: wiping a counter, preparing a snack, straightening toys. Action helps him stay anchored.

In recent sessions, he has begun to describe the cost of living so long with his guard up. He says he is tired in a way sleep does not fix. He misses opportunities to feel present because some part of him is always scanning for danger. Yet he also shows persistence and a deep sense of responsibility. He comes to appointments on time, remembers details from previous conversations, and reflects carefully before he speaks. What stands out is how much of his life has been organized around survival, and how even now he continues to search for places where he can breathe without waiting for the next удар.
